stories.body:
Jenny’s back pain usually settles within a few weeks. This time, 12 weeks have passed and it still intrudes on her life. Getting dressed hurts. Sitting through work is difficult. And something else is becoming harder to ignore: worry.

Why hasn’t it gone away? Is something seriously wrong? Will it ever get better?

Social media offers plenty of alarming possibilities. Jenny starts monitoring every twinge. Each painful movement seems to confirm that something must be wrong.

Jenny is fictional, but her experience may be familiar. When she consults her doctor, she might expect relief from exercise, medication or hands-on treatment. Could the consultation itself also influence her pain?

Imagine two versions of Jenny’s appointment. In one, the doctor interrupts her and describes her back as “worn out”. Jenny leaves with exercises, but also with a disturbing picture of a fragile spine.

In the other, the doctor listens, explores her concerns and examines her carefully. Finding no signs suggesting a serious underlying cause, they explain what they have assessed, acknowledge how disabling her pain is and discuss a manageable plan.

Both appointments might include the same exercises, but Jenny may leave with different expectations about her back.

Researchers call these surrounding influences “contextual factors” . They include expectations, past experiences, the doctor’s communication and the care setting.

Studies suggest these factors are linked to treatment outcomes. In one study involving 182 people with longstanding back pain, a stronger relationship with their physiotherapist early in treatment was associated with better outcomes after eight weeks.

Another UK study involving 960 patients receiving physiotherapy, osteopathy or acupuncture found that the relationship between patient and practitioner was among the strongest predictors of reduced disability. Agreement about treatment goals and how to achieve them was particularly important.

These observational studies cannot establish that the relationship caused improvement, but they suggest that what happens during a consultation deserves attention.

How words can influence pain

If Jenny’s pain is in her back, how could someone’s manner or explanation influence it?

Pain is not a straightforward measure of damage: its intensity does not always match the extent of tissue injury .

One possible explanation comes from predictive processing theories . These suggest that the nervous system interprets signals from the body alongside previous experiences, expectations and present circumstances.

Read more: The surprising science of what pain is and why it hurts

For Jenny, pain that once meant “another episode that will settle” may now mean “something dangerous that nobody has identified”. This change in expectation could contribute to her pain feeling more threatening.

This is one possible explanation of persistent pain. It does not mean Jenny has consciously caused her symptoms.

There is experimental evidence that expectations can influence pain. In one study , healthy volunteers received a powerful opioid painkiller while experiencing painful heat. Positive expectations roughly doubled the drug’s pain-relieving effect, while negative expectations abolished it.

The drug was still being delivered, but participants received different information about it. Brain scans also showed changes in activity in regions involved in processing pain.

This suggests that expectations can influence pain through measurable biological processes. However, findings from short laboratory experiments cannot tell us exactly how much a particular consultation will affect someone with longstanding back pain.

Giving reassurance something to stand on

Simply saying “there’s nothing wrong” is unlikely to address Jenny’s experience. Something plainly is wrong: she hurts, cannot do what she normally does and wants to understand why.

A useful explanation would acknowledge this while distinguishing pain from evidence of serious disease. It would explain the assessment and give Jenny opportunities to ask questions.

The doctor might also ask what she fears. Perhaps her main worry is that bending will damage her spine. Exercises alone may leave that concern untouched.

A theory called “active inference” offers another way to understand this. It proposes that expectations influence what people do, while their actions provide new information that can change those expectations.

In a 2026 paper applying this approach to pain affecting muscles and joints , researchers suggest that movement, communication and other aspects of care may help patients develop different expectations about their bodies.

If Jenny expects bending to cause damage, she may avoid it. With appropriate clinical guidance, gradually exploring that movement could help her discover that her back is more capable than she feared.

This theory may help explain how care works, but researchers have not shown that applying it improves outcomes beyond existing treatments. Treatments also have specific effects that cannot be explained by context alone.

Context has limits

A reassuring consultation cannot replace appropriate assessment or effective treatment, repair an injury or guarantee recovery. Nor does the importance of context justify offering unproven treatments simply because they are delivered with a good bedside manner.

Patients should never be blamed for continuing pain or told they need to think positively.

For doctor, the practical message is to combine careful assessment and evidence-based treatment with explanations that inform without creating unnecessary alarm. UK clinical guidance supports shared decisions, advice about remaining active and individually appropriate treatment for lower back pain.

Patients can reasonably ask what might be causing their pain, whether there are signs of anything serious and what activities they can safely continue.

Jenny needs her pain taken seriously, her concerns heard and a credible way forward. The way that care is offered may help shape what happens next, including her confidence in moving and managing pain.

stories.body:
XpresTest has years of experience conducting disease screening in U.S. airports but has never worked with Ebola or provided biosecurity services abroad. It’s “a new thing for us,” the company’s CEO said.

The Trump administration awarded a small biosecurity company nearly $40 million to screen for Ebola and other infectious diseases just months after a firm linked to President Donald Trump’s elder sons invested in its parent company, according to records and interviews.

The contracts, one to screen for Ebola in several U.S. airports and the other to respond to disease outbreaks in the Democratic Republic of Congo, are seven times the total value of government contracts the company had directly received before.

The company, XpresTest, has years of experience monitoring for COVID-19 and other diseases for the government at U.S. airports. That makes its parent, XWELL, an unusual hybrid, selling both spa treatments and biosecurity services. Last year, it made most of its money from waxing salons and airport spas that offer manicures, massages and “ chakra beds. ”

The contracts are the latest example of the president’s family benefiting financially from his administration’s actions. And the stakes for these deals are particularly high. In the Democratic Republic of Congo, an Ebola outbreak has killed more than 5,000 people this year, and the federal government is trying to stop the pathogen from coming to the U.S.

XpresTest has never worked with Ebola or provided biosecurity services abroad, let alone in the kind of volatile locales it’s now expected to work in. The CEO of its parent company, Ezra Ernst, said XpresTest won both contracts in a competitive bidding process and pointed to its years of experience doing screening for COVID-19 and other pathogens at American airports. But even he acknowledged that working internationally is “a new thing for us” and expressed uncertainty about being able to complete the work in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

“This is a risky contract. I’m not sure we can do it,” Ernst said in an interview.

Jeremy Konyndyk, who helped oversee the U.S. government’s response to a 2014 Ebola outbreak in West Africa, said there are some parallels between monitoring for COVID-19 and Ebola at airports, but he said it’s concerning that the government would award such a lucrative contract to a company that has no experience in Africa.

“There are countless organizations in the world that have decades of experience doing this work,” Konyndyk said. “I have to wonder why the hell they’re not going with someone who has actually done this before.”

Under previous administrations, the U.S. government addressed international disease outbreaks in partnership with the World Health Organization. But Trump withdrew from the group last year, dismantled the U.S. Agency for International Development , which handled much of this work, and dramatically scaled back the global presence of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

At the same time, the State Department launched the America First Global Health Strategy , which calls for the U.S. to use aid to foreign countries to “promote American companies and American innovations abroad.” This March, the State Department announced it would be giving up to $4.5 billion in funding for various purposes, including responding to infectious disease outbreaks.

Under that program, XPresTest was awarded $20 million. Other funding went to better-known global aid nonprofits, including International Medical Corps, Save the Children and the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, whose awards ranged from $25 million to $35 million.

The CDC also awarded XPresTest a contract, for $18.8 million.

In response to questions from ProPublica about XPresTest and its parent company, XWELL, the State Department noted the firm’s previous work screening for diseases at airports under a contract with the CDC and said its own award was made “through a competitive process that builds on this successful model.”

The CDC did not respond to a request for comment.

A spokesperson for the president’s sons Donald Jr. and Eric Trump said that they are “merely passive, minority investors in a fund that invested in this company,” and that they had no “involvement in or knowledge regarding the negotiation or procurement of any of its contracts, including any government contracts.”

“Both are private citizens who hold no government positions, broken no laws and who have every right to pursue lawful business and investment opportunities,” the spokesperson said.

The Trump sons’ connection to XWELL was established in February, when a fund called American Ventures invested in the company. The fund was launched by Dominari Holdings, a small financial firm with offices inside Trump Tower in New York. The leaders of Dominari hired the Trump sons as advisers after their father was elected to a second term and granted them a stake of more than 10% in Dominari.

Anthony Hayes, the CEO of Dominari Holdings, told ProPublica, “We have never seen or even heard of Don or Eric using their family name to influence the granting of a government contract.”

American Ventures has taken stakes in other companies that have benefited from Trump administration actions. The Florida-based drone company Powerus got a contract worth up to $90 million from the U.S. Air Force five months after the Trumps’ involvement was announced. Through American Ventures, Donald Jr. and Eric Trump also are acquiring a stake in a critical minerals group that has received U.S. government support to mine for tungsten in Kazakhstan. The Trumps have described themselves as passive investors who do not advocate for the companies they have stakes in before their father’s government.

XWELL was founded in 2006 as a line of airport-based spas that provided massages and facials. During the pandemic, the company, then known as XpresSpa Group, got $5.5 million from the CDC to offer travelers COVID-19 testing. It also collected waste from airplane toilets to check for new viral strains. It has done similar work for at least one other company that has received government contracts.

In January, XWELL announced that it was hiring a former senior adviser at the CDC who created and led the agency’s traveler surveillance program. The firm said the move was part of a plan to expand “its traveler-based pathogen surveillance capabilities to support international travel hubs and large-scale mass gathering events worldwide.”

The following month, American Ventures invested about $30 million in XWELL. The company had lost money the previous year. “We were so cash-strapped, close to bankrupt,” its CEO said.

Its valuation before the cash infusion was just $3 million. In exchange, American Ventures got a roughly 10% stake in the company to start, with an option to essentially print and sell millions of shares in the future.

Why American Ventures would invest so much in XWELL is unclear. In other cases, when the fund has invested in similar tiny publicly traded companies, some of those firms have moved into hot new sectors and drawn publicity for their connection to the Trumps, then Dominari has offloaded shares. In this case, there is no indication it has sold any of its stake yet.

In June, XpresTest was awarded the CDC contract for what a public notice about the grant said was “Ebola entry screening services.”

XpresTest then received the State Department grant for “rapid, effective, and coordinated outbreak response” to infectious disease threats in the Democratic Republic of Congo, which began in September, according to a government database . The company is also planning to work in Kenya and Morocco. XWELL’s website shows it is now hiring specialists in Ebola response training and biosecurity in the U.S.

In July, after XpresTest was awarded the CDC contract, XWELL announced plans to sell the subsidiary along with its line of spas to a private facial spa company. Ernst, the CEO, said the government contracts played a role in the $13 million sale price and will follow XpresTest to the new company.

That means XWELL, the company that the Trump-linked investment fund took a stake in, will benefit financially from the Trump administration contracts if the sale closes, even though it won’t be involved in doing the work for the government.

XWELL said in a public filing that the sale was part of an effort “to pursue a new direction in the national security sector.” Ernst said he didn’t know the exact plans but thought the parent company might be looking to work with the Department of Defense.

XWELL did not announce either of XpresTest’s biosecurity contracts, which recently became public in federal contracting disclosures. Public companies like XWELL are required to report so-called material events, developments that could affect their share price, such as a large government contract. XWELL has publicized previous work for the federal government, including a $2 million, eight-week pilot program for testing COVID-19 in 2021 .

When asked why his firm didn’t announce the awards, Ernst gave various reasons, including the possibility that XPresTest might wind up not being able to do the work — either because of its own inexperience working internationally or because the Trump administration might suddenly shift priorities and only pay for a fraction of the contract.

“None of these contracts are guaranteed,” he said.

The biosecurity awards add to the questions about the Trump family’s enrichment during his second term. The Trump family’s business activities extend far beyond Dominari and American Ventures. The president himself has made more than $1 billion from cryptocurrency ventures whose value has ballooned as his administration has taken a friendly stance to the industry. And other companies backed by his sons Donald Jr. and Eric have received billions of dollars in federal deals. Earlier this year, ProPublica reported that the Pentagon granted a small North Carolina startup linked to Trump Jr. a $620 million loan after a top aide to the president intervened on the company’s behalf. The Pentagon denied preferential treatment, and a spokesperson for Trump Jr. said he played no role.

The Trumps’ financial ties to government deals and actions are expected to be a primary focus of Congress in the coming months after Democrats won control of both the Senate and the House in last week’s midterm elections.

“When the government is corrupted for personal gain over the public interest, Americans lose trust and taxpayer dollars are wasted,” Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, wrote in a letter to colleagues last week.

stories.body:
A Closer Look

In the year I spent examining Pennsylvania’s troubled legal system, I found that Superior Court judges have blasted lawyers for abandoning clients and judges for mishandling cases. One called a case an “embarrassing saga.”

Co-published with The Philadelphia Inquirer

One morning in July 2025, I was the lone spectator in Judge Frank Palumbo’s courtroom in Philadelphia, watching prosecutors and public defenders haggle over the fates of defendants.

Palumbo paused the proceedings to talk to a lawyer he’d appointed to help a prisoner who had ineptly challenged his conviction. The lawyer profusely thanked the judge for the job. Then, Palumbo offered a bit of guidance: “I think I know where this is going to go. I don’t want to make it overly complicated. It’s real simple.”

The judge said he’d pass along a brief that a different lawyer had filed arguing that there was no merit to the man’s claims in a related case. “I’m not saying plagiarize,” the judge said.

The attorney told the judge he got the message. “So it’s called a Finley letter,” he said, using the common legal term for that no-merit brief, in which an attorney can argue against the client’s claims and ask to withdraw from the case.

“It’s looking like it’s going to be a Finley dismissal,” the judge agreed after a bit more discussion, “but every option is open.”

I’ve spent years covering criminal justice in Pennsylvania, including the post-conviction system that allows people to argue that their lawyer had mishandled their case or to raise newly discovered evidence. That day, I left the courtroom wondering how what I’d observed squared with the state’s promise of effective legal representation in cases like this.

That question sent me on a yearlong reporting odyssey, during which I read hundreds of Finley letters, tracked down court financial records from all 67 Pennsylvania counties, interviewed dozens of lawyers and analyzed thousands of court dockets. What I wanted to know was: Why has it become the norm for Pennsylvania’s lawyers to argue against their own clients? And who is this system serving?

I found that lax rules, low pay and heavy caseloads have compromised legal representation under the state’s Post Conviction Relief Act. Over the past year, I’ve reported on how lawyers, working under fee structures banned in other states, fell years behind on their cases. I spoke with prisoners who’d waited nearly a decade for their lawyers to file anything and others whose lawyers filed Finley letters despite compelling evidence of innocence . I also looked at three years’ worth of invoices and found that, three quarters of the time, Philly lawyers who wrote Finley letters had never spoken with their clients, contacted the trial lawyer or obtained available police files before deciding their claims had no merit.

None of those seemingly basic steps, I was surprised to learn, is required under the law. In fact, dozens of lawyers I spoke to expressed sharply divided opinions about the extent of their obligations to these clients.

But court-appointed lawyers are not working unsupervised. Judges are largely in charge of appointing them to cases, and those same judges are supposed to make sure they’re doing a timely and diligent job.

I noticed that judges continued to assign lawyers more cases even after appeals courts flagged serious issues with their work. And when it came to Finley letters, judges accepted almost all of them over the three years of cases I reviewed, despite the lawyers’ minimal investigative efforts. Some of the letters they approved contained obvious factual errors or even named the wrong client.

Last fall, after Palumbo gave the lawyer a copy of a Finley letter, the lawyer followed the template. His no-merit brief said that his client’s claim could not be considered because he’d missed his filing deadline. The bulk of the document was, in fact, identical to the other lawyer’s brief.

Palumbo, who didn’t respond to my requests for comment, accepted the Finley letter anyway, let the lawyer drop the client and dismissed the claim.

Who Judges Judges?

I thought a fair way to evaluate judges would be to look at the rulings of the Pennsylvania’s Superior Court, the state’s appeals court that hears hundreds of challenges to judges’ rulings on post-conviction matters each year.

And boy, did the Superior Court have thoughts on how judges are handling post-conviction cases.

In one withering opinion, a judge bemoaned an “embarrassing saga” of deficient lawyering that a Berks County judge had tolerated. Another derided a Philly judge and the five attorneys she’d appointed who all missed appeals deadlines, writing, “As Hall of Fame manager Casey Stengel said of the hapless 1962 New York Mets, ‘Can’t anybody here play this game?’”

After logging hundreds of rebukes laid out in Superior Court opinions by hand, I asked some colleagues with data skills to help identify as many of these cases as possible across the last 14 years, the time frame for which opinions were reliably posted online.

We found that the appeals court flagged more than 250 cases in which judges didn’t intervene as lawyers provided what the court labeled ineffective representation: “sandbagging” a client at a hearing, stonewalling a petitioner who’d mailed two dozen letters to the lawyer’s office or filing boilerplate appeals so vague that they doomed their clients’ cases. In hundreds more cases, judges failed to appoint a lawyer at all, held hearings where petitioners went unrepresented or allowed a lawyer to drop a case, leaving the client stranded on appeal. More than 200 times, they oversaw lawyers who abandoned clients, tanking their appeals or stalling their cases for years.

“Judges are in a terrific position to be able to prevent these kinds of injustices,” said Marissa Boyers Bluestine, a longtime post-conviction lawyer who now works at the University of Pennsylvania’s law school.

The scathing reversals aside, the Superior Court affirms about 80% of lower-court rulings. That’s expected given the strict deadlines and complicated rules about how appeals must be filed. The appeals court is also required to defer to the lower court’s factual decisions. And when it reverses due to an error, the recourse is generally limited to ordering a do-over or, on rare occasions, instructing the lower court to explore sanctions. In one opinion, the court resorted to using boldface to call out an egregious failure: “The PCRA court did nothing in this case for 20 years.” Then, it told the lower court to try again.

Judges do have the authority — and, in fact, an obligation under state rules — to make disciplinary referrals. Because complaints are confidential, there is no way to know how often they do so. But only six lawyers in the last decade have been publicly sanctioned for work on court-appointed post-conviction cases.

Judicial discipline is even rarer. No lower-court judge in at least a decade has been publicly disciplined for mishandling a post-trial matter. Judges who, according to the Superior Court, exhibited biases, imposed vindictive sentences or improperly denied recusal requests remained on the bench.

Even after the Superior Court raised alarms, more than 100 cases ricocheted between the appeals court and county judges two, three, four or more times, as judges repeated errors or reappointed lawyers to cases they’d already mishandled .

One such case played out after Jefferson County’s only judge, John Foradora, sentenced a woman to up to 22 years in prison for passing two narcotics pills in prison. Her lawyer failed to object to or appeal the lengthy sentence. After she filed a PCRA, the Superior Court found that her lawyers’ inaction enabled the “ unduly harsh and clearly unreasonable ” punishment to stand. But each time the Superior Court reversed, Foradora again imposed a lengthy term. After three such reversals, the woman wound up serving more than eight years. Foradora said through a court spokesperson that he was unable to comment.

Shannon McDonald, an attorney in the Philly suburbs, said that “some judges don’t consider PCRA a priority.”

She described waiting as a petition languished on a Delaware County judge’s desk for two years, until her client had finished his sentence and been released from prison. Then, the judge finally ruled, dismissing the claim.

The Finley Problem

Like lawyers, judges I’ve spoken with seem to be divided on their obligations, especially when it comes to the no-merit letters known as Finley letters. The state Supreme Court says that when a lawyer submits a Finley letter, the judge needs to conduct a review of the merits of the case.

Attorney Rob Perkins, who leads the nonprofit Allegheny Lawyers Initiative for Justice, told me that while he’s encountered some judges who take post-conviction matters seriously, others seem to view them as a nuisance. He said several lawyers told him that they were afraid that if they litigated cases too aggressively, judges would withhold future assignments. The no-merit letter becomes the simplest path forward: “When a judge is handed a no-merit letter that sounds good, I think their inclination is to accept that the attorney did their job.”

Superior Court opinions reflect this pattern as well. In my review, I found hundreds of cases overruling lower-court judges who accepted flawed Finley letters. The appeals court noted that lawyers claimed, incorrectly, that their clients had missed filing deadlines, rejected legitimate claims as meritless or failed to notice that their clients were serving illegal sentences.

In dozens of cases, judges approved defective Finley letters that did not fulfill basic rules, such as including a notification to the client or addressing all the claims the client wanted to raise.

Several judges told me that Finley letters serve an important purpose, in shutting down frivolous challenges that waste resources.

“Not all [claims] have merit,” Judge John J. Mead of Erie said. “A lot of them initially you could look at and make a determination [as to] whether or not it’s going to require a hearing.”

I’ve noticed that the system makes accepting Finley letters the simplest choice for judges. A judge who rejects a Finley letter must either find a new lawyer willing to take the case, or force the same lawyer to pursue a matter they previously deemed meritless.

Judges who take that path risk pitting a lawyer against his own client, the Superior Court wrote in one recent case, finding the judge’s actions resulted in the denial of a man’s right to counsel. His lawyer, forced to handle a hearing after writing a Finley letter, treated it “ more like a cross-examination of a witness that [he] does not believe than a direct examination of his client.”

Jon Auritt, who retired after more than 50 years as a lawyer in Delaware County, said that these failures stem from a common cause: Instead of working independently, lawyers are beholden to the local judges who appoint them.

Even if judges are not as explicit as Palumbo was with their instructions, Auritt said, their message is often clear: “The judges are never incentivized to appoint a lawyer who might earnestly find a reason to overturn the conviction.”

stories.body:
International development cooperation – external financial and technical support for economic and social improvements in lower-income countries – is shifting fast all around the world. Nowhere is this happening faster than in Africa.

Aid cuts, natural and war-related shocks, unstable geopolitics, rapidly growing young populations and high external debt levels mean African leaders have to find new development paths.

Central to this new agenda is easing dependence on external development finance. Africa has resources of its own – over US$1 trillion in pension assets across the continent, as a recent African Development Bank (AfDB) report highlighted. Much of it is invested outside the region.

Relying more on Africa’s own resources is no easy fix for the region’s many development challenges. But it can reduce dependence on fickle (and hard-currency) external financing. And perhaps more importantly, it signals that African countries want to build a new kind of growth model that is truly “country owned”.

The region’s leading multilateral development bank, the African Development Bank , has been central to driving this agenda under its president, Sidi Ould Tah , who took office in 2025. AfDB’s decades-long trajectory, mix of African and external government ownership and active engagement across the continent mean it can play a key role in the fast-changing development landscape.

Mobilising home-grown financial resources

One of Tah’s initiatives has been aimed at mobilising financial resources from across Africa. This includes the New African Financial Architecture for Development which was supported at the African Union summit in February 2026 and the Africa Forward Summit in Nairobi in May. The bank went on to adopt it later that month.

The ambitions of the initiative are to build a

shared, continent-wide framework for reorganising how capital and risk are mobilised, structured, and deployed across Africa’s financial ecosystem – grounded in the principles of subsidiarity, complementarity, coordination, and risk transformation.

That all sounds very nice. But what does it mean in practice? Is this just another vague declaration of good intentions that will quickly run up against the structural problems that have long held back Africa’s ability to finance its own development?

Early signs are positive. The African Development Bank is launching several practical new initiatives to build up other African development finance institutions. This is a logical first step to more ambitious efforts to join up the regional financial system more broadly.

Scaling up

Sub-Saharan Africa has had a diverse set of multilateral development finance institutions, beginning in the 1970s. The African Development Bank was a shareholder of several and provider of credit lines for on-lending.

For most of their history, they have been relatively modest in scale. Nevertheless, several have begun growing rapidly in recent years. These include the Africa Finance Corporation, the West African Development Bank, African Trade Insurance Agency, Africa Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank) and Trade and Development Bank.

The African Develpment Bank is ramping up its engagement with these institutions. Its aims are: to accelerate their growth; strengthen their ability to mobilise domestic capital sources; and encourage greater collaboration.

The bank has already launched new financial investments and operational agreements with several of them. They include:

an agreement with the Development Bank of Central African States to provide technical support, sub-market credit lines and backing to reinforce its capital base.

joining the Ecowas Bank for Investment and Development as a shareholder and approving a US$70 million credit line to the bank. This was quickly followed by a one-notch bond rating upgrade in August from Moody’s, showing the value of AAA-rated African Development Bank’s backing.

building up the African Trade Insurance Agency to become a pan-African insurance and guarantee provider at a meaningful scale. The African Development Bank has increased its capital share of the agency to 14% of the total (up from 3% in 2025). It also played a role in encouraging Germany and France to become shareholders.

The goal is for the agency to help de-risk African investments for domestic and overseas institutional investors like pension funds and sovereign wealth funds.

New thinking on next steps

The next step is to roll out a new programme to invest in hybrid capital issued by multilateral development finance institutions and, potentially, some national development banks in the region.

Hybrid capital is similar to a regular bond but has attributes that allow it to be counted as equity capital by development finance institutions and by rating agencies.

Hybrid capital is a useful for several reasons:

it is less risky than regular equity

it generates a reliable income stream

it doesn’t have any governance implications, since it does not offer any voting rights

institutions have substantial room to expand its use, as it’s new.

The hybrid programme will start by the end of 2026, targeting several regional development finance institutions.

Another initiative supporting Tah’s agenda is to build a cross-institution securitisation platform with the Development Bank of Southern Africa. Securitisation – turning non-liquid assets like loans into tradeable securities – can allow multilateral development banks to originate loans and then shift them off the balance sheet to willing investors, thus clearing space for more lending. This could:

help development banks recycle risk capital into new projects more quickly

make deals more attractive for investors

potentially bring down costs.

Building up African multilaterals

The key advantage of the development finance institution model is that it is sustainable. A well-run and capitalised one can channel commercial investment to development without needing regular budget injections from member governments.

One hopes that other major multilateral development institutions join the African Development Bank by taking equity stakes and investing in development finance institution hybrids. The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development would be a perfect candidate: it is only now starting to move into sub-Saharan Africa . Joining forces in a committed, systematic way with African development finance institutions, rather than just looking for its own deals, would add to its strategic approach in the region.

The example of the Development Bank of Latin America shows what is possible. Founded in 1970, it was a very small multilateral development bank relying on aid agency largesse in its early history. It now has a AA+ rating, issues bonds in 23 currencies and lends more in its countries of operation than either the World Bank or the Inter-American Development Bank in most years.

The same is possible for Africa’s development finance institutions.

stories.title: How Moscow Is Reacting to the U.S. Midterms
stories.summary: Russian media coverage of the Democratic midterm victory reveals Moscow’s concerns about renewed support for Ukraine amid hopes for political gridlock in Washington. The post How Moscow Is Reacting to the U.S. Midterms appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
U.S. President Donald Trump (R) walks with Russian President Vladimir Putin as they arrives at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson on August 15, 2025 in Anchorage, Alaska. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

Governments across the globe have expressed varied responses to the GOP’s stunning midterm defeat as Democrats are poised to take control of the House and Senate in just a couple of months. Russia’s media outlets have been reporting on the results with a focus on how the altered congressional landscape might impact U.S.-Russia relations, particularly regarding the war in Ukraine. Since Moscow often deploys media statements as trial balloons to gauge which narratives resonate with the public, Russia watchers should take heed of the midterm explanations that are making the rounds of Russian state-owned and pro-Kremlin news services, and what purpose these narratives might serve.

The government-owned news organization RIA Novosti observed that the blue wave heralded the end of Trumpism, concluding, “None of this bodes well for Russia. Full control of Congress will allow the Democrats to push pro-Ukrainian and anti-Russian legislation and to secure funding for Kyiv in the budget. Under Trump, the United States ruled out directly supplying weapons to the Ukrainian Armed Forces. Now, [weapons supplies] will most likely be renewed, and all the president’s initiatives are doomed to fail.”

The pro-Kremlin newspaper Vedomosti tapped political analyst Dmitrii Novikov for his take on the elections, who similarly prognosticated that Democrats will aim to pass legislation committing the United States to providing security guarantees to Ukraine. “If the Trump administration doesn’t avoid this effort,” Novikov warned, “the Democrats in Congress may well try to insert additional obligations regarding Kyiv to the [potential legislation], both in terms of language and additional military and economic aid.”

These observations are not far off from Democrats’ stated intentions. For example, newly elected Democratic senators James Talarico and Abdul El-Sayed, who won Senate races in Texas and Michigan respectively, have both expressed strong support for economic and military assistance to Ukraine, with Talarico arguing that continued aid is a “ cost-saving measure ” and El-Sayed casting the conflict as “ a war between democracy and autocracy ” in a 2022 op-ed. Their position is consistent with Democratic and bipartisan efforts during Trump’s second term to expand Ukraine aid and strengthen sanctions against Russia, many of which met have with GOP opposition. Bills like Rep. Gregory Meeks’s Prohibit Corrupt Russia Oil Deals Act, which seeks to reverse the Trump-brokered diesel agreement with Russia and has already received bipartisan support, are likely to gain momentum in both chambers come January.

However, if a Democrat-controlled Congress succeeds in constraining the president’s policy objectives on Ukraine, Trump may behave more chaotically on the world stage, not least because dealing with opposition is not his forte. Prevented from carrying out his domestic agenda, Trump may well seek to achieve his goals in the foreign policy sphere, where since 9/11 the executive has accumulated more power to pursue its aims, such as heading diplomacy efforts and military operations, with limited congressional involvement. Post-election, Trump has reminded voters of his veto authority, which Congress can only override with two-thirds majorities in both chambers, and which the Democrats do not have.

In its analysis of the U.S. midterms, the Kremlin-aligned Lenta.ru news site made a similar observation , with political analyst Georgii Asatrian predicting that a frustrated American president is more likely to focus on the international arena: “A paradox is possible: the president will try to compensate for his limitations within the country by increased foreign policy activity.’” Political scientist Anastasia Gafarova told Kremlin-aligned Gazeta.ru the same thing : “Given his severely weakened domestic political powers, it seems Trump will try to achieve historic successes precisely in that dimension which is institutionally more vested in the executive branch, namely, foreign policy.”

A far more defiant note was struck by the state-controlled media organization RT, which insisted that U.S. policy toward Ukraine and Russia is unlikely to change. Associate Professor at RUDN University Nikolai Parkhit’ko told RT : “It’s too early to talk about a landslide Democratic victory. […] The Democratic Party has sensible politicians who are discussing reducing aid [to Ukraine] which comes primarily from the pockets of American taxpayers. Kyiv is celebrating right now, as though Ukraine has flown to Venus and the rest of us are all left here to die. But it’s utterly immature and ill-conceived to think that tomorrow Zelensky will be given a trillion dollars, it’s shortsighted.” Although there are no Democrats who publicly discuss reducing Ukraine aid, this sally aligns with similar RT efforts that target U.S. voters as part of wider influence operations that weave populist grievances into pro-Russian narratives, in this case lamenting the loss of hard-earned American tax dollars in order to undermine public support for Ukraine.

The media assessments vary because they serve different purposes. If Russia is unable to achieve its objectives in Ukraine or make dialogue breakthroughs with Washington, it will be convenient to blame Democratic interference and military support for Kyiv. At the same time, the coverage reassures Russian readers that Trump ultimately has final say over U.S.-Russia relations, and even if he didn’t, Moscow’s decision-making does not rely on political shifts in Washington. After all, although Russia has often regarded Trump as useful, its most recent foreign policy concept has assessed that the United States seeks to weaken Russia and undermine its economic and technological capabilities while threatening its sovereignty and territorial integrity.

Finally, the repeated prophecy in pro-Russian news outlets of escalating tensions between the U.S. Congress and a president who, they insist, will be aggressively focused on making unilateral foreign policy decisions that undermine the Democratic agenda, is consistent with the Kremlin’s own preference for American disruption, distraction, and gridlock. The more disunited and dysfunctional the American government is, the less effective it will be in challenging Russian ambitions.

stories.body:
It’s time for a new governing vision.

Nathan Gardels is the editor-in-chief of Noema Magazine. He is also the co-founder of and a senior adviser to the Berggruen Institute.

The great blue wave that washed over America in the election should not lure Democrats into the delusion that they are once again lovingly embraced by the body politic.

Rather, it should be seen for what it is: a widespread counter-revolt at the ballot box against all that Trumpism has wrought — a heightened crisis of affordability exacerbated by trade wars and a war of choice with Iran, self-dealing corruption, politicization of the rule of law and an unbounded, mean-spirited mega-megalomania rarely seen in mature democracies.

The worst mistake Democrats can make is to misread their mandate. That mandate is to narrow the margin of maneuver of a wounded lame-duck presidency, derail the trajectory toward autocracy and clean up the mess. It is not to return to the status quo ante of cultural elitism, censorious identity politics, lax borders and hyper-globalization that opened the path to Trumpism in the first place.

Above all, what Americans are looking for is not so different than what the Gen Z uprisings erupting across Europe and South Asia these days are seeking: to restore trust in the fairness of governing institutions and unclog the routes of opportunity and upward mobility by tackling inequality at the root of the affordability crisis.

With the double failure of the old Democratic agenda and now the Trumpist alternative, the 2028 presidential contest will be the next chance for a new governing vision to emerge in the United States.

Whatever else such a vision may encompass, there are two structural changes that are imperative to ensuring that an anxious and alienated public will have a real say and a clear stake in their future.

First, the only way out of social polarization and the appeal of autocracy is a deeper institutional culture of engagement in which citizens themselves are involved — outside the divisive passions of the partisan electoral arena — in setting the rules that govern their lives. In other words, participation without populism.

Second, mending the fissures of democracy will only be possible if the growing concentration of wealth at the top generated by the arriving AI economy is more widely shared.

We have written about this often in Noema, but I will restate the case in the new context of the latest turn in American politics.

Sharing The AI Wealth

Much of the driving force of politics to come is a pervasive sense of gross inequality, that chances are no longer fair and those with connections and assets are accelerating away from the average family, which is only falling behind with no hope of catching up. Upward mobility has become a mirage. For too many, the good life is receding beyond reach.

Those who revolted against a cultural elite they viewed as looking down on them found themselves faced instead with a politically connected economic elite more entrenched and consolidated than ever before in post-World War II America.

As a result, there is an upswelling reaction from below. Those across America’s various electoral contests voting for “democratic socialists” are not hardened partisans of an old ideology. They are only a broad constituency realizing that capitalism is not working for them; that the benefits of how our system works, supercharged by digital technology, go to those who are already rich and getting richer because they own the assets that are growing in value.

If the pervasive sense of gross inequality is a key driver of social and political division, then the answer is broader wealth sharing so all Americans are pulling in the same direction.

This is where the idea of “universal basic capital” comes in.

AI innovations are increasingly decoupling productivity growth and wealth creation from employment and income, widening the inequality gap between those who “own the robots” and those who labor for their livelihood. Read Noema in print.

The value of productivity growth associated with AI is accruing to those with financial assets that are ballooning on the tail of Big Tech, concentrating wealth at the pinnacle. The top 10% own 93% of all equities.

Despite the immediate post-election market turmoil, regulation on safety and data center-related energy concerns expected from the new Congress will, in the end, temper the justified worries of the public about AI. While slowing down the pace of the race to the frontier of superintelligence, it will incentivize the kind of practical applications we’ve seen in China that will boost productivity across the economy.

A new social contract that responds to this dynamic would foster an ownership share for all in the wealth generated by intelligent machines that portend the displacement of gainful employment and wage depression as AI penetrates the entire economy. After all, it is the general intellect — the public’s personal data — that is the raw material transmuted by algorithms into a productive asset. If wealth is produced by all, all should share in its value.

“The worst mistake Democrats can make is to misread their mandate.”

This can be done mostly through universal savings/investment accounts for families and individuals seeded by an innovation levy on companies across the AI economy. The idea is not only to break up concentration of wealth at the top but to also build it from below. The best way to fight inequality in the digital age is to spread the equity around.

Thinking Outside The Ballot Box

The connective tissue of democracy has seriously decayed in recent years as trust in impartial institutions has hit rock bottom and the public square splinters into social media silos.

The triumph of Trumpism was not the cause of this crisis of governance. It was a symptom of the decay of democratic institutions that, captured by the organized special interests of an insider establishment, failed to address the dislocations of globalization and the disruptions of rapid technological change. To add danger to decay, the fevered partisans of populism all too readily threw out the baby with the bathwater, assaulting the very integrity of institutional checks and balances that guarantee the enduring survival of republics. The revolt against a moribund political class transmuted into a revolt against governance itself.

Since neither the stakeholders of the old status quo nor the upstarts of populism have offered any effective, systemic solutions to what ails the nation, protracted polarization and paralysis set in.

In the end, there are only two solutions to this predicament — the move Trump has made toward strongman autocracy, or thinking outside the ballot box by inviting the broader civil society into governance through new mediating institutions of citizen engagement that complement representative government.

One reparative response, embryonic but indicative of the larger possibility, has been introduced in California: a first-in-the-nation online public platform to help bridge silos and mend the breach of distrust between the public and the institutions of self-government. The platform, called Engaged California (EC), encourages and facilitates the direct engagement of citizens with government and with each other.

Engaged California is not glorified polling and is more than a town hall gathering. It is a three-way tool that enables policymakers and administrators to listen at scale to average citizens outside of election cycles and be responsive; it invites citizens to directly voice their concerns and proposals on an ongoing basis; and it is a platform for Californians from all walks of life to interact with each other to find common ground.

AI serves as a sorting tool to register consensus among thousands of participants on priorities for government action and to collate fresh ideas that emerge from this practice of collective intelligence.

In short, it is exactly this kind of innovative institutional platform for “governing with the people” that can restore trust because the public itself is proactively engaged.

Beyond Tinkering

Since the great transformations underway in America today are systemic in nature, so too must new ways and means of governance go beyond tinkering around the edges of waning ways that no longer fit the times.

Governance is how communities invent and shape their destiny. It determines whether a society goes forward or backward. Like the homeostasis of all organisms, governance is the regulator, arbiter and navigator of human affairs. It processes emotions through reason, as the means by which societies not only survive but thrive by adapting to change.

Going forward in this light, democratic practices and institutions must adapt to the unprecedented scale of connectivity in a way that fosters a governing consensus instead of dividing the body politic against itself. In an AI economy, where massive new wealth is being generated by mining the general intellect of public data and transforming it into a productive asset, the old industrial division between labor and capital diminishes and everyone must become an owner sharing fairly in that wealth.

With the old slate now wiped clean by failed alternatives, the space is opening once again for the political imagination to think anew with a systemic response to the challenges at hand. The blue wave rebuke of Trumpism puts the onus on Democrats.

The ambition of the 21st century should no longer be to maximize growth, but to maximize prosperity.

Philipp Humm is an artist, author and ex-tech CEO living in Milan.

More than 2,000 years ago, Aristotle formulated one of history’s most remarkable thought experiments. What, he asked, would happen if tools could obey commands, even anticipate them? What would happen if they could carry out their work entirely on their own?

“If every instrument could accomplish its own work, obeying or anticipating the will of others,” he wrote in “Politics” around 350 B.C.E., “if the shuttle would weave and the plectrum touch the lyre without a hand to guide them, chief workmen would not need servants, nor masters slaves.”

For centuries, this passage was understood primarily as a philosophical allegory. Today, what is striking is not Aristotle’s technical imagination but his political imagination. He was more interested in the social consequences of self-operating machines than in their feasibility.

Artificial intelligence forces us to confront this issue anew: What becomes of a society whose economy, purpose and welfare state are built on wage labor if wage labor loses that foundational role? Perhaps the true AI revolution will begin in our conception of what it means to be human, not inside Silicon Valley’s data centers.

More Or Less?

What’s better: more people or less work for humans? Few contradictions capture our historical moment more precisely. Never before has a society simultaneously spent so much money attempting to compensate for labor shortages while investing so much in technologies designed to eliminate labor altogether.

If current fertility rates continue and net migration falls to zero, United Nations projections suggest that many Western populations will shrink by about 30% by the end of this century. In countries such as Italy, the decline approaches 40%-50%. Governments have responded with generous family subsidies and large-scale immigration programs but have seen limited economic success. Research suggests that immigration’s fiscal contribution depends heavily on education, employment, age at arrival and migration motive. Highly skilled migrants, the minority, tend to generate net economic gains, whereas low-skilled immigration, the majority, can impose a net fiscal drag on advanced welfare states.

In Britain, falling fertility, population aging and migration have become inseparable topics. Parliamentary debates frequently frame birth rates as a long-term growth problem. At the same time, the government seeks to reduce reliance on migrant labor by expanding domestic training programs. In the United States, similar arguments are made from the opposite side: Economists warn that the native-born labor force is shrinking and that immigration now supplies much of America’s labor-force growth. Also, a new Silicon Valley pronatalism has emerged. Elon Musk, Peter Thiel and other technology leaders warn that collapsing birth rates threaten civilization, even as their companies build systems designed to reduce the economy’s dependence on human labor.

In addition to trying to stabilize the size of their labor force, governments invest aggressively in artificial intelligence to stay internationally competitive. The labor displacement that these technologies will ultimately produce is often ignored or dismissed with reassuring promises that new jobs will inevitably emerge, as they always have in the past.

“Perhaps the true AI revolution will begin in our conception of what it means to be human.”

The management of this contradiction is even more striking in East Asia.

South Korea, with a fertility rate of around 0.75 children per woman, is experiencing a demographic collapse unprecedented in peacetime. The government spends tens of billions each year on birth and family incentives and housing programs designed to reverse the trend. So far, little success. Simultaneously, South Korea has become the most robot-intensive economy in the world with over 1,000 industrial robots per 10,000 manufacturing workers.

Japan presents a similar picture. Its working-age population has been declining for more than two decades, and the country has responded by pursuing one of the world’s most ambitious automation and robotics strategies. Today, Japan possesses one of the highest densities of industrial robots with more than 400 per 10,000 manufacturing workers, compared to the world average of around 120-150.

South Korea and Japan offer a preview of the intelligence economy. Their governments are investing in automation to compensate for shrinking workforces while trying to arrest population decline to preserve domestic demand and the fiscal foundations of their welfare states. Both policies make sense within the industrial economy. But what happens when AI and robotics reduce the economy’s dependence on human labor? Could demographic decline and automation eventually become complementary rather than opposing forces?

The Invention Of Homo Faber

The labor society as we know it today is not an anthropological constant. For most of human history, people were not primarily Homo faber — the productive individual who derives social worth from economic work. They became so only with the rise of modernity, and above all through the Industrial Revolution.

In classical antiquity and most of medieval Europe, manual labor was regarded as a necessity performed largely by slaves and the lower classes. The privileged classes devoted themselves to politics, philosophy, religion, war, arts and leisure. As Hannah Arendt observed in “The Human Condition” (1958), modernity radically overturned the classical hierarchy of human activities. Labor, once regarded as a necessity of life rather than its purpose, increasingly became the organizing principle of society.

Adam Smith provided the intellectual economic foundation for this transformation. In “The Wealth of Nations” (1776), he argued that the true wealth of a nation lies in the total productive labor of its people, not in gold, land or trade surpluses.

Around 1800, roughly 75% of Americans worked in agriculture. Today, fewer than 2% do. America’s industrial transformation created an entirely new economic logic, one symbolized by Henry Ford’s famous wage increase in 1914. Ford understood that his workers should build automobiles and earn enough to buy them. That insight captured the genius of industrial capitalism: production, wages and demand were bound together.

“If artificial intelligence assumes an increasing share of productive labor, society will have to find answers to how to cultivate lives that remain meaningful outside employment.”

This model was at the core of Western democracies throughout the 20th century. Wages financed taxation, welfare systems and pensions. At the same time, they generated income that sustained consumption and served as the principal mechanism of social integration. In numbers, labor accounts for up to 60% of GDP and private consumption for nearly 70% for OECD nations.

The importance of wages extends far beyond the hours people spend at work. Every productive hour finances about nine hours of non-working life: the years of childhood, education and retirement; evenings, weekends and illnesses. Another way to look at it is that every hour of paid work supports those hours of non-working life across society, including workers’ own time outside employment and that of children, students, retirees, homemakers and other dependents. Historically, these ratios have increased, driven mainly by reductions in working hours and increases in life expectancies.

When jobs become scarcer or wages lose their economic bargaining power, this architecture begins to fracture. This puts immense pressure on public finances: Children, retirees, students, the sick and much of public spending ultimately depend on the wages of the working population.

The defining economic problem of our century so far has been How does a society finance ever more years of life with ever fewer years of work? For decades, advanced economies have managed to answer that question through a fragile combination of economic growth and rising public debt. But what happens when artificial intelligence begins to undermine the labor market on which that answer rests?

When Intelligence Becomes Cheap

Every major technological revolution transformed a scarce factor of production into an abundant one. The Industrial Revolution dramatically reduced the cost of mechanical energy with fossil fuels. Globalization in the 1990s and 2000s lowered the cost of physical labor by integrating China and other emerging economies into global production networks. The AI revolution may now do the same with intelligence. Cognition, coordination, pattern recognition and many forms of decision-making could become abundant rather than scarce resources.

John Maynard Keynes anticipated this possibility almost a century ago. In his 1930 essay “Economic Possibilities for our Grandchildren,” he warned of what he called technological unemployment: the possibility that humanity might discover ways of saving labor faster than it could discover new uses for it.

For decades, economists largely dismissed this concern in two ways. The first was Joseph Schumpeter’s theory of creative destruction. Technological progress destroys existing occupations, but it also creates new industries, new professions and ultimately more productive forms of employment. The second was historical experience. Every previous technological revolution had ultimately generated more people employed, not mass unemployment.

With AI, this historical adjustment mechanism may no longer be applicable.

The Stanford economist Erik Brynjolfsson has described this possibility as the “Turing Trap.” Previous generations of machines primarily replaced physical labor in a few defined routines. Human beings remained one step above the machines, becoming their planners or problem-solvers. That historical shock absorber is now shrinking. AI is increasingly performing many of the cognitive activities that once enabled workers to move up the value chain.

MIT’s Daron Acemoglu arrived at a similar conclusion from a different direction. He argues that the key issue is how firms choose to deploy AI. If businesses use AI primarily to replace workers rather than to augment their productivity, the historical pattern of technological progress creating more employment than it destroys might no longer hold. The structure of the emerging AI economy already reflects this logic. Many of today’s most valuable AI companies generate extraordinary market value with remarkably small workforces.

Agentic AI further accelerates this process. Agents no longer automate isolated tasks; they increasingly perform entire workflows: analyzing information, correcting errors, adapting strategies and coordinating complex processes with minimal human intervention.

“For the first time since the Industrial Revolution, labor could cease to be the economy’s scarcest factor of production.”

For companies, the decisive issue is simple: Can AI perform economically valuable tasks at substantially lower cost than humans? Increasingly, for many roles, the answer is yes.

The substitution of labor by machines is unfolding in two waves.

The first affects white-collar work. A junior financial analyst, lawyer, management consultant or software engineer in London or New York may cost an employer 80-100 per hour. Modern language models can already perform many of their tasks for a fraction of a cent. Systems possess another structural advantage. While the knowledge accumulated by an employee spreads only gradually through an organization and often disappears when that employee leaves, improvements made by software are retained and deployed instantly and at scale across an entire system.

The second wave is now reaching the physical economy and the blue-collar population. Humanoid robots developed by companies such as Tesla and China’s Unitree are learning increasingly complex movements through observation and simulation. Their manufacturers hope eventually to reduce operating costs to below $2 per hour. This is in stark contrast to 30-50 per hour for an average American worker.

Research by the International Monetary Fund suggests that nearly 60% of jobs in advanced economies will be affected by artificial intelligence, with almost half facing substantial disruption or substitution. Against that background, a reduction of roughly 30% in total employment over the coming decades no longer appears implausible. Whether the final figure is 20% or 40% is ultimately of secondary importance.

What matters is that, for the first time since the Industrial Revolution, labor could cease to be the economy’s scarcest factor of production. If that is true, the consequences extend far beyond the labor market. They force us to reconsider one of the deepest assumptions of the industrial age.

Shrinking Rich

It is precisely at this point that a possibility emerges that remains almost unthinkable in the discourse today: Population decline, discussed almost exclusively as an economic catastrophe, may prove to be an essential corrective during the intelligence revolution. I call this the 30/30 equilibrium.

The idea is simple. Imagine an advanced economy whose population gradually declines by around 30% over several decades while artificial intelligence and robotics reduce labor demand by a similar magnitude. These developments will not occur simultaneously or at the same pace, yet over time they could broadly offset one another. Fewer people require fewer jobs. As a result, the historical ratio between productive labor and the total population could remain remarkably stable without placing an additional burden on public finances.

The 30/30 equilibrium is, first and foremost, a theory of macroeconomic stabilization in which demographic decline ceases to be an economic disaster and becomes part of the adjustment mechanism. However, it does not create prosperity.

Whether a shrinking society also becomes richer depends on a second variable: capital deepening. As the Solow-Swan growth model demonstrates, long-run prosperity depends less on the size of the labor force than on the amount and productivity of capital available to each worker. If AI and robotics increase productive capital faster than the labor force contracts, output per person continues to rise even while the total workforce declines. Read Noema in print.

If we want an economy’s GDP to stabilize, we need a booster. A 30% decline in the labor force would have to be offset by roughly a 45% increase in capital productivity. This would raise GDP per capita by more than 40%. Given the learning curves already observed in semiconductors, computing power, artificial intelligence and robotics, together with the widening cost advantage of machine intelligence over human labor, such productivity gains no longer appear particularly ambitious.

Now, suppose instead that the population remained constant while productive capital increased by the same 45%. Total output would then expand by roughly 20%. Conventional economics would celebrate this as the superior outcome.

William Stanley Jevons observed in the 19th century that more efficient steam engines did not reduce Britain’s coal consumption. They increased it. As energy became cheaper, new applications emerged, further expanding demand.

Efficiency produced abundance, but abundance also produced greater resource use. The same dynamic may now apply to intelligence. As AI becomes cheaper, we will almost certainly consume far more of it. This applies to cognitive work as well as to robotics. Silicon Valley celebrates this future as “abundance.” Yet abundance is not necessarily environmentally sustainable. Every additional product made and consumed at a fraction of today’s cost and price still consumes energy and leaves a negative ecological footprint. In addition, AI systems require substantial electricity, computing infrastructure, rare materials and manufactured hardware. Abundance comes at a high cost to the physical world.

“For the first time in history, we may be able to become fewer without becoming poorer. We may even become richer while placing a lighter burden on the natural world.”

From an environmental perspective, allowing the population to decline naturally while increasing prosperity per person may therefore represent a superior equilibrium. For the first time since the Industrial Revolution, the intelligence economy offers us the possibility of choosing such an equilibrium.

This requires abandoning two assumptions inherited from the industrial age.

The first is financial. Modern economies are organized around debt, money creation and asset valuations that all depend on continual expansion. Tomorrow’s economy must become larger than today’s because yesterday’s obligations must be repaid. A “shrinking-rich economy” may ultimately require a monetary and financial system that derives its stability less from ever-expanding debt than from the growing productivity of capital.

The second is geopolitical. “Big is beautiful” belonged to an era in which economic and military strength depended directly on scale. Larger populations meant more workers, more consumers, more inventors, larger armies, bigger markets and greater geopolitical influence. The intelligence economy changes that logic. Human intelligence is scarce, but artificial intelligence expands usable intelligence at an extraordinary pace and cost, making it an abundant resource. Furthermore, technologies such as autonomous drones increasingly erode the traditional military advantages of scale. The same is true for economic influence.

Ecology offers a useful framework. The ecologist Eugene Odum distinguished between pioneer and climax ecosystems. Young forests grow aggressively, consume resources and prioritize speed over sustainability. Mature forests grow little yet contain far greater biomass, complexity, stability and resilience than the pioneer systems from which they emerged.

Human civilization may not be fundamentally different. The fossil-fuel economy was humanity’s pioneer phase. Its success rested on expansion: more people, more energy, more production and more consumption. Artificial intelligence, combined with demographic decline, might allow advanced societies to enter a different stage of development. Technologies such as robotic recycling, AI-managed precision fermentation and closed material loops already point toward an economy capable of creating greater prosperity with fewer material inputs.

The resulting climax society would not be a society of sacrifice. It would be a society that has learned to distinguish growth from prosperity. For the first time in history, we may be able to become fewer without becoming poorer. We may even become richer while placing a lighter burden on the natural world.

The ambition of the 21st century should no longer be to maximize growth but to maximize prosperity: to shrink rich.

Who Inherits The Loom?

If the intelligence economy delivers the productivity gains its advocates expect, it will generate unprecedented wealth. This raises the central political question of the post-labor age: Who receives the surplus?

Under the existing economic order, the answer is clear. The gains will accrue primarily to the owners of capital, not to labor, as ownership determines who has a claim on output. If AI and robotics replace labor as the decisive productive force, then income will shift away from wages and toward those who own the machines, models, data centers, energy systems and platforms through which the new economy operates.

This creates a problem even for the capital owners. Henry Ford understood that workers were producers and consumers. They had to earn wages sufficient to buy the cars they manufactured. The same logic applies to the intelligence economy but in a more unstable form. If machines produce goods while human beings lose the wages with which to buy them, the demand side of the economy weakens. Even the most productive AI economy ultimately depends on customers who can afford to buy what it produces.

Silicon Valley’s preferred answer to this problem is universal basic income (UBI). The idea is simple. The state provides citizens with a minimum income funded through higher taxes, increased public debt or levies on automated production. In the short term, some form of income floor may well be necessary. It could stabilize demand as the population shrinks and cushion the social shock of technological displacement.

But as a permanent settlement, UBI risks becoming a pharmakon: remedy and poison at the same time.

If financed through public debt, UBI injects additional money and purchasing power into the economy without increasing the supply of productive assets, creating inflationary pressure that erodes part of AI’s productivity gains. If financed by taxing production, businesses will ultimately recover much of the additional cost through higher prices, with a similar effect. In both cases, a significant share of the productivity dividend is dissipated rather than translated into higher real living standards.

Economic history offers a warning. In 1795, English magistrates introduced the Speenhamland system, a wage supplement designed to protect rural workers from poverty. It was intended as relief. In practice, it subsidized employers who could continue paying low wages while the public purse made up the difference. It also entrenched the poor’s dependence on local authorities.

The analogy is not exact, but the lesson matters. Income support may ease the transition, but it is unlikely to provide a durable foundation for a post-labor economy.

“What kind of human beings do we wish to become?”

The challenge, therefore, is to distribute the productivity gains of the intelligence economy without eroding them. That requires a financing mechanism that is neither debt-financed nor production-tax-financed.

Here, Karl Marx becomes newly relevant, though perhaps not for the reasons usually assumed. In the “Grundrisse,” he imagined a future in which wealth would no longer depend primarily on immediate labor time, but on the technological appropriation of what he called the “general intellect”: the accumulated knowledge, science and cooperative intelligence of society. Marx’s most contemporary insight was his recognition that knowledge would become the decisive productive force.

Artificial intelligence gives this idea a literal technological form. AI models are not created in a vacuum. They are trained on the accumulated intellectual inheritance of humanity: books, scientific papers, Wikipedia entries, forum discussions, software libraries, images, public archives, open-source code and countless traces of human communication. They also depend on publicly funded research, energy infrastructure, universities, telecommunications networks, roads, water systems and legal protections. The intelligence economy is built by both private firms and a civilizational commons.

Therefore, should the returns from these systems accrue exclusively to private owners, or should society retain a claim on the productive infrastructure that emerged from its collective knowledge?

The 20th century solved the demand problem through wages. Silicon Valley proposes to solve it through transfers. The intelligence economy may ultimately solve it through ownership.

Society’s claim to a universal capital dividend, instead of a UBI, could take the form of ownership, where governments would secure equity stakes, public stakes or sovereign wealth claims in AI infrastructure that depends on public resources, public data and public markets to operate. The proceeds would not flow into general budgets but would instead be distributed directly to citizens as a universal dividend.

Ownership operates differently economically and is not inflationary. It distributes the productivity gains directly at their source, preserving the full efficiency gains of automation while broadening participation in the wealth it creates.

The former wage-earning seamstress would become a shareholder in the loom rather than a dependent of the state. Aristotle imagined a world in which the self-weaving loom abolished the necessity of labor. The intelligence economy gives us the opportunity to decide who inherits it.

The Devil In Paradise

Suppose we succeed. Imagine that artificial intelligence performs most productive labor, demographic decline cushions the adjustment, a new ownership model distributes the gains of automation without sacrificing productivity and advanced societies once again live within ecological limits. Humanity would come remarkably close to Aristotle’s vision of the self-weaving loom. We might finally become Homo curans.

Even then, two deeper challenges remain. The first concerns meaning. More than 70 years ago, Arendt warned of the danger of what she called “worldlessness.” A society organized around work does not automatically become a society of free citizens once work disappears. On the contrary, people might lose the shared public realm in which they experience responsibility, judgment and a sense of purpose. The deeper crisis of the post-labor age may therefore not be unemployment, but meaninglessness.

The anthropologist David Graeber reached a similar conclusion from a different direction. His analysis of “bullshit jobs” suggested that much contemporary employment does not survive because it is socially indispensable, but because modern societies have forgotten how to organize meaning outside paid work.

If artificial intelligence assumes an increasing share of productive labor, society will have to find answers to how to cultivate lives that remain meaningful outside employment.

The second challenge is even more far-reaching. As the world becomes more complex, we increasingly delegate decisions to artificial intelligence. At first, AI merely assists human judgment. Soon it recommends. Eventually, it decides. Every delegation begins as a convenience and may end in dependency. Human judgment gradually atrophies through disuse.

This process is already visible. We delegate navigation to algorithms, communication to recommendation systems, information retrieval to search engines, financial decisions to automated models, partner selection to matching applications and increasingly even legal and administrative decisions to AI-assisted systems. Each individual delegation appears rational. Together, they transform the relationship between human beings and judgment itself.

The logic of intelligent machines is not identical to the logic of human beings. Their purpose is optimization. Ours is judgment. Confusing the two may ultimately prove to be the deepest alignment problem of all.

As these systems increasingly surpass us in specialized domains, the risk is less that they become human than that humans gradually surrender their own capacity for judgment. We may discover too late that we have become second-class decision-makers in a world optimized by machines: Homo algorithmus.

More than 2,000 years ago, Aristotle asked what would happen if the shuttle could weave by itself. Today, that is a reality. But the self-weaving loom leaves us asking: What kind of human beings do we wish to become? Whether the intelligence economy gives rise to Homo curans or Homo algorithmus will not be decided by technology, but by us.
